segments.en: Kia ora. That is the Māori greeting you will hear from airports to school playgrounds, and it wishes you life and good health. In Māori, this land is called Aotearoa, often translated as the land of the long white cloud.

The Māori people arrived by voyaging canoe from eastern Polynesia many centuries ago, finding their way by the stars, the winds and the swell of the ocean. Their language, Te Reo Māori, is an official language here.
You may see a haka performed before a rugby match or at a wedding or a farewell. It is a powerful ceremonial dance with stamping feet and chanting voices, and it expresses pride, welcome and respect.
Visiting a marae, a Māori meeting ground, begins with a formal welcome. Afterwards you may share a hongi, gently pressing noses and foreheads with your host, sharing the breath of life.

The landscapes change fast. In the north there are bubbling mud pools and steaming geysers around Rotorua. In the south, the Southern Alps rise snowy and sharp above glaciers, fjords and bright blue lakes.
Wellington, the capital, sits at the windy southern tip of the North Island, while Auckland, the biggest city, is spread across old volcanic hills between two harbours.

Because these islands were cut off for so long, many unusual birds live here. The most loved is the kiwi, a shy, round bird that cannot fly and comes out at night to poke for worms with its long beak.
The bird is so loved that New Zealanders call themselves Kiwis too, and the fuzzy brown fruit took the same name.

For a feast, many families cook a hāngī, where food is placed on hot stones in a pit in the ground and left to steam slowly. Pavlova, a meringue cake piled with cream and fruit, is a favourite summer dessert.
Rugby is close to a national passion, and the national team, the All Blacks, is famous around the world. Netball, cricket and sailing are hugely popular too.
At the start of winter many New Zealanders celebrate Matariki, the Māori New Year, when a cluster of stars rises in the dawn sky. It is a time to remember loved ones and plan for the year ahead.
Before you go, stand on a beach at sunrise and look out across the Tasman Sea. Ka kite anō, see you again, and across that water Australia is waiting for you.
